clue.text: Quit drugs and start to sew on retirement

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the assembled letters run backwards

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone gives up drugs and takes up needlework in retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quit drugs' reads as one phrase, but 'Quit' is the definition on its own and 'drugs' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit something is to cease doing it; both verbs mean bring an activity to an end.

clue.text: A sense of discernment

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the five senses, alongside sight and smell
second meaning: good judgement in matters of style

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, 'a sense of discernment', but 'of' is only a link between two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the faculty of perceiving flavour and also refined aesthetic judgement, as in having good style.

clue.text: Piece of crockery on a posh table

parts.note: a dish to eat from
taken as written
U means upper-class in crossword convention

explanation.surface: A dinner plate set down on an upmarket dining table.
explanation.walkthrough: The table here is not furniture but a geographical one: tableland. In a down clue, 'on' puts the dish above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is an area of high flat ground, also called a tableland or table in geography.

clue.text: Hallowed ground: can't cross over area

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed and broken up, so its letters are reshaped

parts.note: the word without its apostrophe
taken as written
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A sign on sacred land warning that you cannot walk across this area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hallowed ground' looks like a single noun phrase, but 'Hallowed' alone is the definition and 'ground' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sacrosanct is regarded as too sacred or holy to be violated or interfered with.

clue.text: A shade unhappy? Toughen up!

parts.note: to steel is to toughen; in a down clue 'up' also places it at the top
feeling blue is feeling sad

explanation.surface: Someone a little down is told to stop moping and harden up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shade unhappy' reads as 'slightly sad', but 'A shade' is the definition, a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel blue is a dark greyish-blue colour, so it is one particular shade or hue.

clue.text: Reddish-brown ape's biting repelled salesman

indicators.note: a mouth that bites closes around what it takes, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: to ape someone is to imitate them

indicators.note: to repel is to drive something back, so these letters face the other way

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: A rust-coloured ape bites a salesman who had been driven away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reddish-brown ape' suggests an orangutan, but the colour is the definition and the ape is a verb meaning mimic.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper metal has a reddish-brown colour, so a coppery shade is this tint.

clue.text: Old nasty type and earl release gas in public

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a rat is a contemptible person
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: An unpleasant old man and an aristocrat break wind in front of everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude surface is a joke: 'gas' is hot air, empty talk, so releasing it in public is making a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to speak pompously at length to an audience, often dismissed as spouting hot air.

clue.text: Some steamer I caught in a foreign country

indicators.note: some of something is only a part of it, so the letters sit inside a longer run

parts.note: a run of letters across these three words

explanation.surface: Travelling abroad, a passenger catches a steamer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' looks like part of the story, but the letters run straight through it.
explanation.definitionFit: The United States is a country, and to a British setter and solver it is a foreign nation.

clue.text: Friendly and agreeable sort of conga line

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version of it, so the letters come out in a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A party conga line is a sociable, good-natured kind of dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-word definition can feel like padding, but both adjectives together describe the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A congenial person or place is pleasant, sociable and suited to one's tastes.

clue.text: Willy Nelson's last on as he messed with a speaker!

indicators.note: things messed with are thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled
the last of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: closing letter of the name
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The country singer Willie Nelson fiddles with a loudspeaker on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willy Nelson' poses as the singer; 'Willy' is split off as a jokey adjective meaning relating to Will, the playwright William Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespearean means relating to William Shakespeare, nicknamed Will, so 'Willy' is a mock adjective for his works.

clue.text: Grass repeating the same crimes gets caught

indicators.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a serial offender commits the same crime again and again

explanation.surface: An informer, a grass, keeps committing the same offences until arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: A grass is British slang for a police informer, which the surface leans on; here it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereals such as wheat, oats and barley are cultivated species of the grass family.

clue.text: One bringing out lamps for ship's watch? Au contraire!

indicators.note: French for 'on the contrary', telling us the two parts sit the other way round from their wording

parts.note: to eye something is to watch it
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: Someone fetches lanterns for the night watch aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamps' is slang for eyes, and to bring them out is to make them stand out. 'Ship's watch' gives the two parts, which the French tag puts back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeliner is make-up drawn round the eyes to accentuate them, and lamps is old slang for eyes.

clue.text: Pretend friend gets you locked up in reality

indicators.note: someone locked up is shut inside, so one piece goes within the others

parts.note: to act is to pretend
text-speak spelling
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: An imaginary friend lands you in jail once real life catches up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretend friend' reads as one imaginary companion, but splits into two pieces, and the U goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbial: actually means as a matter of fact, truly, as opposed to seemingly.

clue.text: Way to be overlooked by conservative crowd

indicators.note: what is overlooked sits below the thing looking down on it, so in a down entry the other piece comes first

parts.note: Con is the abbreviation for Conservative
a course is a route or way

explanation.surface: A path goes unnoticed by a crowd of traditionalists.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'overlooked by' puts the second piece above the first, so the conservative comes on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A concourse is a gathering or throng of people, as well as the open space where they assemble.

clue.text: Pitiable time with, possibly, Havana revolutionary

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a Havana is one example of a cigar, hence 'possibly'

explanation.surface: A sorry period in Cuba alongside a Havana rebel, perhaps Che or Fidel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Havana revolutionary' summons Castro, but Havana is the cigar and 'revolutionary' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragic describes something causing great sadness, deserving pity and sorrow.

clue.text: Club together at The Fringe on meal with pound off

indicators.note: a fringe is a border, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

indicators.note: something taken off is removed, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: a luncheon is a formal midday meal
L is the abbreviation for pound sterling

explanation.surface: Pooling resources for a meal at the Edinburgh Fringe festival, without paying full price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club together' looks like chipping in, but 'Club' alone is the definition, a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A truncheon is a short thick stick carried by police officers, a kind of cudgel.

clue.text: Boy crossing through southern border in a tense state

indicators.note: crossing through a word strikes it out, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a son is a male child
S is the abbreviation for southern
an edge is a border or rim

explanation.surface: A lad crosses a southern frontier during a nervy standoff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossing' suggests travel across a frontier, but it means striking a letter out.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on edge is an idiom for being nervous, jumpy and anxious.

clue.text: Call famous matchmaker on the mobile to create problem

indicators.note: on the phone we only hear words, so these are judged by sound

parts.note: to call is to dial, and Emma is Jane Austen's meddling matchmaker

explanation.surface: Phoning a celebrated matchmaker leads to trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma Woodhouse, heroine of Jane Austen's novel Emma, is fiction's best-known matchmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is a difficult situation requiring a choice between unwelcome alternatives.

clue.text: Groups who govern people pleading in hearing

indicators.note: what is in someone's hearing is what they hear, so the word is taken by sound

parts.note: counsels are barristers who plead cases in court

explanation.surface: Governing bodies listen to people making appeals at a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' suggests a court session, fitting the barristers, but it is also the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Councils are elected bodies that run local government affairs, such as town or county administrations.

clue.text: Take heed outside parking by trade union

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round the others

parts.note: to heed is to take care
P is the sign for a car park
TU is the abbreviation for trade union

explanation.surface: Be careful outside the car park next to the union offices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take heed' reads as a single warning, but 'Take' is the definition and 'heed' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To capture is to seize or take something by force, such as a prisoner or territory.

clue.text: Fabulous Greek geezer who's a bit of a nag in part

definitions.text: Fabulous Greek geezer who's a bit of a nag in part

parts.note: surface reading: a great Greek bloke who can be rather a nag at times

parts.words: a bit of a nag in part
parts.note: setter's reading: a mythical creature that is partly a horse

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means from fable, 'geezer' is British slang for a man, and a nag is an old horse, not a scold: half man, half horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Centaurs in Greek myth have a human upper body on the body and legs of a horse.

clue.text: Sweet kitty taking medicine rolled around

indicators.note: something rolled round has turned over, so the letters run back to front
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a kitty is a pool of shared money
a tablet of medicine

explanation.surface: A lovely cat swallows a tablet and rolls about on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet kitty' suggests a cute cat; 'Sweet' is the definition and the kitty is a fund of shared money.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a hard boiled confection on a stick, so it counts as a sweet in British usage.

clue.text: Beastly type together with cutting secretary

indicators.note: a blade cutting something goes into it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: PA is a personal assistant
'and' joins things together

explanation.surface: A brutish person teams up with a sharp-tongued secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly type' sounds like a nasty person, but it means a type of beast, an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The panda is a bear native to China, so it is one kind of animal or beast.

clue.text: One dancing in the low-lit breezy night?

definitions.text: One dancing in the low-lit breezy night?

parts.note: surface reading: a person dancing in a dim, windy evening
setter's reading: a small flame flickering in a draught

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing' is what a flame does when it flickers, and the 'low-lit' night is lit only by it.
explanation.definitionFit: A wax light's flame wavers and flickers in a draught, which is described as dancing.

clue.text: Young woman getting over stockholder?

parts.note: a lass is a girl, chiefly northern British
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A young woman recovering from her time as a shareholder.
explanation.walkthrough: A stockholder sounds like a shareholder, but the stock is livestock and the holder is a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a looped rope cowboys use to catch and hold cattle, which are stock.

clue.text: Normal manure spread about Saints' first XI?

indicators.note: something spread about is scattered, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Ordinary fertiliser is scattered over the pitch before Southampton's starting team play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First XI' looks like a football team (Saints is Southampton FC's nickname), but 'XI' is the definition, eleven written the Roman way.
explanation.definitionFit: XI is how eleven is written in the ancient numbering system using letters, so it exemplifies the answer.

clue.text: Eastern American head of college keeps learner informed

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a dean heads a college or faculty
L is the learner-driver plate
aware means in the know

explanation.surface: An American college principal on the East Coast keeps a student up to date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastern American head of college' reads as one person, but the definition stops at 'American'.
explanation.definitionFit: Delaware is a state on the US east coast, so a native or resident there is an eastern American.

clue.text: Filled with bit of ire, go off and scream

indicators.note: a vessel filled with something holds it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: food that goes off rots

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small part, here just its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone fills up with anger, explodes and yells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scream' suggests yelling, but here it is something hilarious, a sense shared with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns describe a hugely funny person or event: 'she's a scream', 'he's a riot'.
